claims.text: At tag stage-0, docs/team/sprint-example.md contains a sprint backlog row reading `Nút "Hủy đơn" trên màn hình đơn hàng` with 3 in its `Ước lượng` column, the column in which that table records the team's estimate of the work.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang docs/team/sprint-example.md at stage-0, table header line 12 and row line 15

claims.text: At tag stage-0, docs/team/story-example.md holds one story sentence, five numbered acceptance criteria and a Definition of Done checklist of exactly five lines.
In docs/team/sprint-example.md the junior's third daily sentence is a blocker: not knowing whether an order in state `shipped` may be cancelled, and needing the product owner to answer.
The story in docs/team/story-example.md names who (a customer), what (cancel their own unpaid order) and why (not having to phone the hotline after changing their mind), in one sentence.
That same file states that a story is a promise of a conversation and not a specification, and that an unclear point is asked about before coding rather than guessed at.

This team attaches its acceptance criteria to a single story and agrees them before starting the work; its retrospective names doing so as what went well, because it did not have to do the work twice.

Without acceptance criteria, two people sizing or judging a story are working from two different readings of it, so any size or any claim that it is finished means different things to different people.

Work that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be considered part of an Increment, the usable piece of product the sprint hands over; passing a story's own acceptance criteria does not by itself make the work done.
claims.source_hint: Scrum Guide 2020, Increment and its commitment (Definition of Done)

claims.text: Criterion 1 of the file: when an order is in state `new` and belongs to the customer, the order detail screen shows the "Hủy đơn" button.

Criterion 3 of the file: when an order is in state `paid`, `shipped` or `cancelled`, the "Hủy đơn" button is not shown. No criterion in the file says whether a `shipped` order may be cancelled by the request itself.
Criterion 4 of the file: calling the cancel API for an order that does not belong to the caller returns 403 and changes nothing.
Criterion 5 of the file: cancelling the same order twice returns 409 on the second attempt and the order stays in state `cancelled`.
All five criteria open with `Khi` (when): a condition — a state of the order, or something the customer does — before naming what the system does about it.

The file's five Definition of Done lines: code read and approved by at least one other person; an automatic test for every criterion; runs on the test environment, not only the author's machine; no new build warnings; API document updated.
The retrospective in docs/team/sprint-example.md names writing acceptance criteria before coding as what went well, and gives as the reason that the team avoided doing the work again.
The name Definition of Done is the one the Scrum Guide uses: a formal description of the state the Increment must be in to meet the quality measures required for the product.
claims.source_hint: Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done

claims.text: In the Scrum Guide the Definition of Done belongs to the Scrum Team, or to the organisation where the organisation sets one as a standard, and is stated once against the Increment rather than written per Product Backlog item.
claims.source_hint: Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done

claims.text: The Scrum Guide 2020 uses neither the term user story nor the term acceptance criteria, and prescribes no format for a Product Backlog item beyond saying refinement adds details such as a description, order and size.
claims.source_hint: Scrum Guide 2020, full text; Product Backlog and Product Backlog refinement

claims.text: In docs/team/sprint-example.md the row `Ngừng gửi thông báo cho đơn đã hủy` is the only one whose final status is `Chưa xong, chuyển sprint sau`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang docs/team/sprint-example.md at stage-0, table lines 14-18

claims.text: When the answer is held by someone else, ask: the team's note tells you to ask before coding rather than guess, its sprint note names the product owner (who decides what is wanted) as the one who must answer the blocker, and its retrospective credits writing criteria first with not redoing the work.

Because the sentence records why the customer wants it and not only what they asked for, this team's note treats the story as a promise of a conversation rather than a specification — the asked-for solution stays open to discussion.

In HTTP, 403 is the status code for a request the server understood and refuses to fulfil; 409 is for a request that could not be completed because of a clash with the current state of the target resource.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 sections 15.5.4 (403 Forbidden) and 15.5.10 (409 Conflict); refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt
